name: Sɛlɛɛ
confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand descriptions agree (2 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_citation: Agbetsoamedo, Yvonne. 2014. Aspects of the Grammar and Lexicon of Sɛlɛɛ. Doctoral thesis in Linguistics (comprehensive summary, 100 pp.), Stockholm University. DiVA diva2:742036, FULLTEXT02.
catalog_quote: According to Allen (1974, 111), Sɛlɛɛ has four distinctive phonetic tones: high (H), mid (M), low (L2) and extra low (L1), and “there is no phonologically significant downstep or downdrift” (see Allen 1974, for an extensive discussion of tonal behavior in context). Lexical words in isolation may contain one, two or three of these tones but the possible sequences are restricted. Tones are used in Sɛlɛɛ for lexical contrast, as illustrated by the sets of minimal pairs in (1), and also for grammatical function, as in (2) and (3) below. ... It is evident from the above examples that tones function in ways similar to grammatical morphemes in the language. Currently, Sɛlɛɛ is the only language among the GTM languages known to me to have four tones.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.citation: Agbetsoamedo, Yvonne. 2014. Aspects of the Grammar and Lexicon of Sɛlɛɛ. Doctoral thesis in Linguistics, Stockholm University (DiVA diva2:742036), comprehensive summary, section 2.1.4 Tones.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (100 pp., text, Acrobat 2014). extracted text of p. 33 (printed p. 14) gives section '2.1.4 Tones' with the quoted passage word for word: 'According to Allen (1974, 111), Sɛlɛɛ has four distinctive phonetic tones: high (H), mid (M), low (L2) and extra low (L1), and "there is no phonologically significant downstep or downdrift".. Lexical words in isolation may contain one, two or three of these tones but the possi-ble sequences are restricted. Tones are used in Sɛlɛɛ for lexical contrast, as illustrated by the sets of minimal pairs in (1), and also for grammatical function, as in (2) and (3) below.' The only difference is the line-break hyphen in 'possi-ble'. The section continues on…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Selee is described as a tone language with four level tones (H, M, L, extra-low) carrying lexical and grammatical contrasts; neither this description nor Maddieson & Gordon (1996: 151, 'Sele is a tonal language with lexical contrasts both in nouns and verbs depending on tonal differences') says anything about word stress, accent or prominence, so no stress placement rule can be stated from the accessible sources.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any accessible source.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: Agbetsoamedo notes possible tone sequences on words are restricted and that Selee appears unique among GTM languages in having four non-derived tones; Maddieson & Gordon suspect Heine's contour tones are derived and that Allen's extra-low is in complementary distribution with low.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical words in isolation; nouns and verbs); tone also used for grammatical marking in verbal paradigms (tense/aspect, negation). Agbetsoamedo's four-tone inventory is explicitly taken over from Allen 1974: 111, so that part is second-hand within a first-hand description.
new_statements.identity_note: Both opened sources describe Sɛlɛɛ/Sele of Santrokofi (villages Benua, Bume, Gbodome, north of Hohoe, Volta Region, Ghana) = sele1249 [snw]; no dialect split reported. The name 'Sele' (Maddieson & Gordon) and 'Sɛlɛɛ'/'Selee' (Agbetsoamedo, Glottolog) refer to the same language. The tone inventory quoted from Agbetsoamedo is explicitly credited to Allen 1974: 111.

new_statements.quote: Ihre Aussprache und Tonbezeichnung ist die gleiche wie im Avatime (siehe Mitteilungen Jahrg. XII, S. 288 f.). [p. 183] ... Die Tonbezeichnung erfolgte hier wie in der Avatime-Grammatik S. 289 (Mitteil. Jahrg. XII). [p. 185]
new_statements.translation: Their [the vowels'] pronunciation and tone notation are the same as in Avatime (see Mitteilungen vol. XII, pp. 288 f.). ... The tone notation here followed the Avatime grammar, p. 289 (Mitteil. vol. XII).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File present (45 pp. Rendered pp. 2 and 4 (scans 00000201/00000203 = printed pp. 183, 185) and read the page scan: p. 183, under 'Erster Teil. Die Laute. 1. Die Vokale', prints exactly 'Ihre Aussprache und Tonbezeichnung ist die gleiche wie im Avatime (siehe Mitteilungen Jahrg. XII, S. 288 f.).'; p. 185, last lines after 'Lautveränderungen', prints exactly 'Die Tonbezeichnung erfolgte hier wie in der Avatime-Grammatik S. 289 (Mitteil. Jahrg. XII).' (the ALTO text has scanned splits 'To nbezeichnung' / 'Avatime-Graminatik'; the print is clean). Read pp. 182-186 in full: the sound section covers vowels, diphthongs, consonants, consonant clusters (constant and 'zufällige'), and sound changes;…
new_statements.relation_note: Consistent with the catalog's 'tone language, no stress statement' reading from Agbetsoamedo 2014 (and with Maddieson & Gordon 1996 'Sele is a tonal language'): the 1911 sketch treats the language as tonal (tone marks, Tonbezeichnung) and is silent on stress. It adds nothing on stress placement; it does not contradict anything. Identity: pp. 182 'nur noch in drei Ortschaften mit zusammen kaum 1500 Einwohnern', self-name 'bale' = Balɛɛ = sele1249 (Agbetsoamedo's Benua, Bume, Gbodome). Note Glottolog's hh.bib entry for this reference is tagged language code 'Sekpele [lip]' (sekp1241); the text itself is Santrokofi = Sɛlɛɛ, so that Glottolog tag is an error.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule: the sketch marks tones on words throughout (bombó, bámba, kúnku, tsyóntsyo..) and refers the compiler to Funke's Avatime grammar (MSOS XII, 1909, pp. 288-289) for what the marks mean; it never mentions Betonung, Akzent, Nachdruck or word stress. The phonology part (pp. 183-185) covers vowels, diphthongs, consonants, clusters and sound changes only; the one prosodic remark besides tone marking is that no 'accidental' consonant cluster follows a long syllable (p. 184), which is about syllable weight, not stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Funke's 'Santrokofisprache' is the language of the three Santrokofi villages (about 1,500 speakers in 1911), self-name 'bale' (Balɛɛ), i.e. Sɛlɛɛ sele1249 / snw; the same three villages (Benua, Bume, Gbodome, north of Hohoe) are named by Agbetsoamedo 2014 and Maddieson & Gordon 1996. Glottolog's hh.bib attaches this reference to Sekpele (sekp1241, Likpe), which the text contradicts. Bibliographic correction: the article is in MSOS Jahrgang XIV (1911), not 13(3).

sources.citation: Maddieson, Ian & Matthew Gordon. 1996. Notes on the phonetics of Sele, with particular attention to vowels. UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 93 (Fieldwork Studies of Targeted Languages IV): 149-163. (Glottolog lists it as WPP 95, 1997; the volume itself is No. 93, Dec. 1996.)
sources.note: Sec. 2.3 Tones, p. 151: 'Sele is a tonal language with lexical contrasts both in nouns and verbs depending on tonal differences'; five tones after Heine (H, M, L level plus falling/rising contours), Allen's extra-low treated as a variant of low; authors call their own tone transcription impressionistic. No mention of stress, accent or prominence in the paper (scanned of all 15 pages).

sources.citation: Moran, Steven & Daniel McCloy (eds.). 2019. PHOIBLE 2.0: inventory 'Sele (GM 1330)', contributed by Christopher Green & Steven Moran from Allen 1973 (Sele data sheet, West African Language Data Sheets). Jena: Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History.

sources.note: Second-hand phoneme inventory extracted from Allen's 1973 WALDS data sheet: 33 segments = 18 consonants, 12 vowels and 3 tonemes, high ˦ (U+02E6), mid ˧ (U+02E7) and low ˨ (U+02E8), none marked marginal. It thus encodes Sele as a three-level tone language, one level fewer than the four (H, M, L, extra-low) that Agbetsoamedo 2014 reports after Allen 1974: 111 — a discrepancy worth noting against the catalog statement.
